newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean stocks soar, but not for long say brokers.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean stocks soar, but not for long say brokers.

text.p: South Korean stocks soared on Thursday, sending the leading index up by almost five percent, after the finance ministry urged public pension funds to buy into the depressed market.
But brokers said the request on Wednesday to managers of the three largest pension funds smacked of desperation and the rally was likely to fizzle out early in the new year.
"It's a temporary phenomenon," said Richard Samuelson, the head of reasearch at SBC Warburg in Seoul.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see prices fall back after January 1."
A finance ministry official denied the government was putting pressure on the funds to bail out the market, which has lost 22 percent of its value since the beginning of the year.
Rather, the request to buy a combined 300 billion won ($355 million) worth of stock was a way to help fund managers overcome internal controls and enlarge tiny stock portfolios, the official said.
"It's like Koreans, they won't sing unless you ask them to," said the official, who declined to be named.
The composite stock index jumped at the opening bell and ended the day 29.58 points, or 4.47 percent, higher at 690.97. It was the biggest single-day gain this year.
Individual investors were the biggest buyers, snapping up blue chips on expectations that the funds would comply with the request.
There was no evidence of pension fund buying yet, brokers said.
Samuelson said the finance ministry move was a ruse to dress up the balance sheets of listed banks by boosting their share prices before books close at the end of the year.
Several banks are planning to issue Global Depository Receipts next year. Such issues are contingent on the banks' share prices remaining above certain levels.
"This all helps banks massage their reported earnings," Samuelson said.

Bank stocks have been among the worst performers this year, reflecting a general economic downturn that has slashed profits at leading corporations and prompted a string of bankruptcies among smaller companies.
Daniel Harwood, Regional Director of HG Asia, said foreigners were now net sellers of South Korean stock and the latest rally would not lure them back.
"I'm not picking up the phone and telling clients to jump in," he said, although he added that he believed the market was "a bit oversold".

The finance ministry official said the National Pension Fund was asked to purchase 150 billion won worth of shares, the Government Employees' Pension Fund 100 billion, and the Korea Teachers' Pension Fund 50 billion.
But he denied the government was pressuring the funds.
"Pension funds want to invest in the stock market, but there are a number of internal guidelines that made it difficult for them," he said.
"We're just making it easier for them."
"If they don't want to buy stocks, they'll say no and that's the end of the story," he said.

The National Pension Fund said it had one trillion won in stocks, representing 4.8 percent of its assets. The Government Employees' Fund has 480 billion won in the market, 7.9 percent of its assets. The Teachers' Fund has 180 billion won invested in shares, or 6.0 percent of its assets.

"Today's rise is definitely short-term, but the good news is that the government has shown a strong will to support the market above 660," said Jay Kwon at Hanwha Securities. (Conversion $1 = 844 won)
